warmup.q: The payments app keeps copies in two regions, Europe (EU) and the US, and the link between them has been down since 08:30. At 09:00, the EU copy changes the bank account that shop M-0042 is paid into. At 10:00, the US copy changes the same field. Both clocks are exactly right. When the link comes back, which statement is right?
options: The US change came an hour later, so it should replace the EU one
The two changes are concurrent: neither region knew of the other's, so keeping only the 10:00 one silently loses the EU change
They only clash if they were made within the same second
With perfect clocks, keeping the later write is always correct
warmup.why: Whether one write may replace another depends on whether its writer had seen the other, not on the clock. The US region changed the field without knowing about the EU change, so the US write doesn't include it. Keeping the later write, a rule called last write wins, would keep 10:00 and drop the EU change without anyone deciding to. Perfect clocks only make "later" well defined; they don't make it the right answer. The first section turns this into a test.

sections.h: Concurrent writes: neither one knew about the other
sections.html:
Leaderless replication ended with two people writing the same balance at nearly the same moment, and the replicas keeping only the write with the later timestamp. Many leaders met the same problem between regions. Before we choose a rule for such writes, we need a precise test for when two writes happen "at the same time". The clock turns out to be the wrong tool.

Take three events for one card payment, pay-81723, in the payments app. The app keeps copies in three regions, parts of the world where it runs its own computers: Europe (eu), the US (us) and Asia-Pacific (ap). A card payment usually takes two steps. First the shop asks the card's bank to set the money aside, which is called authorizing. Later the money really moves, which is called capturing. A void cancels a payment before it's captured.

At 10:00:00.000, the eu region authorizes the payment. At 10:00:00.002, the us region, which has already received the authorization, captures it. At 10:00:00.001, the ap region, which has heard of neither, voids it. By the clock, all three happened within 2 ms (thousandths of a second). By what each writer knew, they differ completely. The capture's writer had seen the authorization, so the capture builds on it, and replacing the authorization with the capture loses nothing. The void's writer had seen neither. The void doesn't include the capture, and the capture doesn't include the void.

Leslie Lamport, a computer scientist, named this relation in 1978: happens-before. Write A happens before write B if B's writer knew about A when it wrote. That can be because the same program did A first, because a message carried A to B's writer, or through a chain of such steps. Two writes are concurrent when neither happens before the other. Concurrency is about knowledge, not time. Two laptops that each edit a shop's record while offline, an hour apart, made concurrent writes. Two writes 2 ms apart are ordered if a message got through in between.

The relation says exactly when a store may throw a version away. If A happens before B, B's writer saw A, so B can replace A. That's the normal case, and most writes are like it. If A and B are concurrent, each holds something the other lacks, and any rule that keeps only one of them loses a write. Those are the conflicts of Many leaders, and the rest of this lesson is about finding and merging them.

How does a store know what a writer had seen? The simplest way, which the lab in Many leaders used, is to carry it. Every write lists the ids of all the writes its writer knew about, and A is before B when A's id is in B's list. It works, but the lists grow with every write: in that lesson's steady-traffic run, one write carried 597 ids. The third section shrinks the list to one counter per replica. Ordering without a shared clock: logical clocks and IDs, in the Faults, time and truth track, builds the general tools, Lamport's clocks among them.

Every version carries what its writer had seen. One write may replace another only if it saw it. Two writes that didn't see each other are concurrent, and something has to merge them, or one is lost. Next, we'll look at the most common rule that doesn't merge, and count what it loses.

try.title: Order four pairs of writes without looking at the clock
steps: Read HappensBeforeDemo.kt. It has five writes, each with its clock time and the set of writes its writer had seen.
For each of the four pairs it prints, predict: happens before, happens after, or concurrent? Then run it from the labs folder. No Docker needed.
try.expect:
eu:1 (authorize pay-81723, 10:00:00.000) vs us:1 (capture pay-81723, 10:00:00.002)
    clock gap +2 ms: happens before: us:1 saw it, so us:1 may replace it
us:1 (capture pay-81723, 10:00:00.002) vs ap:1 (void pay-81723, 10:00:00.001)
    clock gap -1 ms: CONCURRENT: neither saw the other; keep one and the other is lost
eu:1 (authorize pay-81723, 10:00:00.000) vs ap:1 (void pay-81723, 10:00:00.001)
    clock gap +1 ms: CONCURRENT: neither saw the other; keep one and the other is lost
laptop:1 (M-0042 payout account, 09:00:00.000) vs eu:2 (M-0042 payout account, 10:00:00.000)
    clock gap +60 min: CONCURRENT: neither saw the other; keep one and the other is lost

The pair 2 ms apart is ordered, because a message carried the authorization to the capturing region first. The pair an hour apart is concurrent: the laptop was offline, and the eu office never heard of its edit. The clock gap predicts neither. Add "laptop:1" to the office write's seen set and run it again: the last pair becomes happens before, with the same hour on the clock.

sections.h: Last write wins drops confirmed writes, and Jepsen counted them
sections.html:
The cheapest rule for concurrent writes is last write wins (LWW). Every write carries a timestamp, and every replica keeps the value with the highest one. The copies always end up equal, because every replica makes the same comparison, and the rule is everywhere. Cassandra settles every value in a row this way (Wide-column stores with Cassandra). DynamoDB global tables, which keep a copy of a table in several regions, settle every item this way in MREC mode, where every region takes writes (Many leaders). So does pgactive, an add-on that lets several PostgreSQL servers take writes. Its cost follows from the first section. For two concurrent writes, "last" only means whichever clock read higher, and the other write disappears without an error.

How much does that lose? In 2013, Kyle Kingsbury measured it on Riak, a leaderless store like Dynamo, as part of Jepsen, his series of tests that break databases on purpose. Clients added numbers to a set stored under one key. Each client read the set, added its number and wrote the set back, which is called read-modify-write. At the end, the test counted which of the acknowledged additions, the ones confirmed to the client, were still there.

With last write wins and no network fault at all, 1,434 of 2,000 acknowledged writes were lost: 71.7%. With a network partition, a broken link that splits the nodes into groups, 1,815 of 1,985 were lost, 91.4%, and strict quorums, with R + W > N and no stand-ins, didn't help (91.7%). The same test with Riak keeping concurrent versions side by side, as siblings merged into one set, lost none of 2,000. The clocks were fine in the first run. Concurrent read-modify-writes were enough.

Leaderless replication quoted Dynamo's own number: 99.94% of cart requests saw a single version. Both numbers are right. Real shopping carts rarely have two writers on one key at once, while every Jepsen client hammered the same key. How much LWW loses depends on how often writes collide; whether it can lose at all depends on the rule. The lab in Many leaders drew the curve: 1% of acknowledged writes lost with writes 5 seconds apart, 38.5% at 50 ms.

Clocks make it worse. With a skewed clock, one that runs fast or slow, LWW can drop a write that isn't even concurrent. A later decision stamped by a slow clock loses to an earlier one stamped by a fast clock. NTP, the protocol computers use to set their clocks over the network, keeps servers within milliseconds of each other on a good day. After a virtual machine (a computer simulated by software) pauses, or a time source goes bad, they can be much further apart. If the Java driver, the library Java programs use to talk to Cassandra, stamps writes on the app's own server, a server whose clock runs 5 seconds fast wins every argument for 5 seconds. The Try it does exactly that: a void issued after a capture loses to the capture.

LWW is safe in one case: a key that is written once and never updated, such as a new record under a fresh random id. Anywhere else, decide whether losing one of two writes is acceptable before you choose it. Next, we'll make the store notice the clash instead of hiding it.

try.title: Lose a void to a fast clock
steps: From the labs folder, start Cassandra on one node: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml up -d --wait (one to two minutes). If the payments keyspace doesn't exist yet, load it: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-02-payments.cql.

Open Cassandra's shell with docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml exec cassandra cqlsh and run the statements below. USING TIMESTAMP sets a write's timestamp by hand, in microseconds since 1970, so you can play each server's clock. Predict the status before the SELECT. Then stop Cassandra: docker compose -f env/cassandra.yml down -v.

code.title: in cqlsh
code.html: -- one table, two app servers: server 2's clock is 5 seconds fast CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments.payment_status (payment_id text PRIMARY KEY, status text); -- real time 10:00:00. Server 2 captures the payment and stamps it with its clock: 10:00:05 UPDATE payments.payment_status USING TIMESTAMP 1794045605000000 SET status = 'CAPTURED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81723'; -- real time 10:00:02. Server 1, whose clock is right, voids it: the later decision UPDATE payments.payment_status USING TIMESTAMP 1794045602000000 SET status = 'VOIDED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81723'; SELECT payment_id, status, WRITETIME(status) FROM payments.payment_status WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81723';

try.expect:
payment_id | status   | writetime(status)
------------+----------+-------------------
  pay-81723 | CAPTURED |  1794045605000000

The void, issued two seconds after the capture, lost to the capture's skewed timestamp. Both statements succeeded, no error appeared, and every replica would agree on CAPTURED. WRITETIME(status) shows the timestamp that won. USING TIMESTAMP plays the part of each server's clock here; in a real app, the Java driver supplies it.

sections.h: Version vectors notice the clash that last write wins hides
sections.html:
Carrying every writer's full list of seen ids works, but the list grows forever. One observation shrinks it. Say each replica numbers the writes it takes in, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and a writer that has seen eu's 7th write has also seen the six before it. Then the list only needs the highest number seen from each replica. That's a version vector: [(eu, 7), (us, 3)] means "has seen eu's first 7 writes and us's first 3". The Dynamo paper calls the same structure a vector clock, and the lab's file keeps that name. Strictly, a version vector tracks the versions of one piece of data, while a vector clock orders events in general.

When a node, call it Sx, takes in a write, it starts from the vector of the version the client read, and adds 1 to its own entry. To compare two versions, compare them entry by entry, treating a missing node as 0. If every entry of A is at most B's, A is an ancestor: B's writer saw it, so A can go. If each has an entry bigger than the other's, the versions are concurrent.

The Dynamo paper walks through this with a shopping cart. Versions D1 and D2 are written through node Sx, so D2 is [(Sx, 2)]. Then two clients both read D2 and write at the same time, one through node Sy and one through node Sz. D3 is [(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)], D4 is [(Sx, 2), (Sz, 1)], and neither is an ancestor of the other. Dynamo keeps both as siblings, versions stored side by side, and returns both on the next read. The client merges the two carts and writes D5 through Sx. With it, the client sends the context, the merged vector of what it read, so D5 gets [(Sx, 3), (Sy, 1), (Sz, 1)]. That descends from both siblings and replaces them.

The stepper runs a shop's list of blocked cards, the opening's two tills grown into two regions, three ways: last write wins, version vectors, and the data type of the next section. Version vectors find conflicts, but they don't settle them. Your code gets the siblings and has to merge them, and the obvious merge has a flaw the stepper shows. A set union, every card that's in either list, brings deleted cards back.

Vectors also grow with every node that takes in a write. Dynamo cut them at about 10 entries, at the risk of losing track of which version came from which, which the paper says never showed up in production. Next, we'll remove the merge code altogether.

frames.say: The link comes back. With last write wins, the replicas compare clock times and keep the later value whole. EU wrote at 10:00:05 by its clock and US at 10:00:03 by its own, so US's version disappears, and with it the block on card-5310. There's no error and no log line. If EU's clock was a few seconds fast, the "later" write wasn't even later.

frames.say: Version vectors don't trust clocks. Compare the two entry by entry: EU's counter for eu is bigger, and US's counter for us is bigger. Neither vector is less than or equal to the other in every entry, so neither write saw the other. They're concurrent, and Dynamo keeps both as siblings for the program to merge, as in its D1 to D5 example.

A missing card can mean "removed" or "never added", and the union can't tell which. That's the Dynamo paper's own warning about the shopping cart: an added item is never lost, but a deleted item can come back.

try.title: Replay Dynamo's D1 to D5
steps: Run the version vector demo from the labs folder. Before it prints, write down D3's and D4's vectors yourself, and D5's after the client merges.
Then compare [(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)] with [(Sx, 3)] in your head. The demo doesn't print that pair; check your answer against the drill.
try.expect:
D1 written by Sx            [(Sx, 1)]
D2 written by Sx            [(Sx, 2)]   D1 vs D2: BEFORE: the second one saw it, drop it
D3 written by Sy (read D2)  [(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)]
D4 written by Sz (read D2)  [(Sx, 2), (Sz, 1)]
D3 vs D4: CONCURRENT: neither saw the other, keep both
a client reads both, merges the carts, sends context [(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1), (Sz, 1)]
D5 written by Sx            [(Sx, 3), (Sy, 1), (Sz, 1)]
D3 vs D5: BEFORE: the second one saw it, drop it
D4 vs D5: BEFORE: the second one saw it, drop it

D3 and D4 each have an entry the other lacks, so they're siblings. D5's vector is at least as big as both in every entry, so it replaces them. The context the client sent back is what told the store that D5 had seen both siblings. Without it, the store would have no way to know which versions the new write replaces.

sections.h: CRDTs: data types that merge in any order without losing a write
sections.html:
Merging siblings by hand is where conflict handling usually breaks. What if the data type knew how to merge itself, so that any two copies combine into the same result, in any order, and no write is lost? That's a CRDT, a conflict-free replicated data type. The idea is easiest to see with a counter.

Say the app counts shop M-0042's pending payouts, the payments waiting to be sent to the shop, in three regions while the links between them are down. Version 1 gives each replica one running total, and merging two copies adds their totals. That counts some payouts twice. Once eu has merged us's total, the next sync between them adds us's payouts a second time, and a copy that reaches eu by two paths counts twice too.

Version 2 is the G-Counter, a grow-only counter. Every replica owns one slot and only ever adds to its own. The value is the sum of the slots, and two copies merge by taking the bigger number in each slot. A slot only grows, so the bigger number is always the newer one, and taking it twice changes nothing. To count down as well, keep two G-Counters, one for additions and one for subtractions, and take one total from the other. That's a PN-Counter, for positive-negative.

Taking the bigger number works because it has three properties. The order of merges doesn't matter (it's commutative), the grouping doesn't matter (associative), and repeating a merge changes nothing (idempotent). Any merge with all three lets replicas swap copies whenever they can, by any path, as often as they like, and still end up equal. No clock is involved, and nobody waits for anyone.

Sets are harder, because removals are where unions fail. The OR-Set (observed-remove set) tags every add with a unique tag, such as us:1. A remove records the tags of that element it has seen, and only those. An element is in the set if it has a tag nobody removed. Merging is two unions, of tags and of removed tags. A remove beats the adds it saw, and an add made at the same time somewhere else, which it couldn't see, survives. In the Try it, one region unblocks card-4417 while another blocks it again, and after the merge, it's blocked.

CRDTs have limits that matter for money. Their extra data grows: a slot per replica, a tag per add, and removed tags kept forever unless the replicas agree to clean them up. And they fit only operations whose order doesn't matter. "A balance never goes below zero" isn't one. Two regions can each approve a 600 payment from a balance of 1,000, and both counters merge happily to -200. A rule like that needs replicas that agree before they write, which the Transactions track and the Consistency and consensus track cover.

CRDTs suit counts, sets, on-off flags and documents that several people edit. In Jepsen's test, the run that lost nothing merged Riak's siblings as a set, one of the simplest CRDTs, and Riak 2.0 later built CRDTs in as data types. The text editors of Local-first software and sync engines use them for documents.

One question this track has left alone: which values a read may return in the first place, and what "strongly consistent" really promises. That's where the Consistency and consensus track begins. First, the Try it merges three regions' copies in every possible order.

try.title: Three regions diverge, then merge in every order
steps: Read CrdtDemo.kt. Three regions edit a PN-Counter of pending payouts and an OR-Set of blocked cards while they're cut off from each other.
Predict the merged count and the merged set before you run it. Then run it from the labs folder. No Docker needed.

code.title: CrdtDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.repl.l08.demo /** A PN-Counter: per-replica slots of increments and of decrements. Merge takes each slot's maximum. */ private data class PN(val p: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap(), val n: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap()) { fun add(r: String, by: Long) = if (by >= 0) copy(p = p + (r to (p[r] ?: 0) + by)) else copy(n = n + (r to (n[r] ?: 0) - by)) val value get() = p.values.sum() - n.values.sum() fun merge(o: PN) = PN(maxed(p, o.p), maxed(n, o.n)) private fun maxed(a: Map<String, Long>, b: Map<String, Long>) = (a.keys + b.keys).associateWith { maxOf(a[it] ?: 0, b[it] ?: 0) } } /** An OR-Set: element -> tags of its adds, plus the tags removed. Merge is two unions. */ private data class OR(val adds: Map<String, Set<String>> = emptyMap(), val removed: Set<String> = emptySet()) { fun add(e: String, tag: String) = copy(adds = adds + (e to (adds[e].orEmpty() + tag))) fun remove(e: String) = copy(removed = removed + adds[e].orEmpty()) val elements get() = adds.filterValues { tags -> tags.any { it !in removed } }.keys.sorted() fun merge(o: OR) = OR((adds.keys + o.adds.keys).associateWith { adds[it].orEmpty() + o.adds[it].orEmpty() }, removed + o.removed) } /** Every order in which three copies can be merged, by name. */ private fun <T> orders(copies: Map<String, T>, merge: (T, T) -> T): List<Pair<String, T>> { val n = copies.keys.toList() val perms = listOf(listOf(0, 1, 2), listOf(0, 2, 1), listOf(1, 0, 2), listOf(1, 2, 0), listOf(2, 0, 1), listOf(2, 1, 0)) return perms.map { p -> p.joinToString(" + ") { n[it] } to p.map { copies.getValue(n[it]) }.reduce(merge) } } /** * Three regions are cut off from each other. Each keeps taking writes: the merchant's pending-payout * counter and its blocked-card set. Then the partition heals and the copies merge, in every order. */ fun main() { // the state every region had before the partition val counter0 = PN().add("eu", 5) val blocked0 = OR().add("card-4417", "eu:1").add("card-9921", "eu:2") // during the partition, each region edits its own copy val counters = mapOf( "eu" to counter0.add("eu", 3).add("eu", -2), // 3 payouts queued, 2 paid "us" to counter0.add("us", 4), // 4 queued "ap" to counter0.add("ap", -1), // 1 paid ) val sets = mapOf( "eu" to blocked0.remove("card-4417"), // eu unblocks card-4417 "us" to blocked0.add("card-4417", "us:1").add("card-5310", "us:2"), // us reports it again, and blocks another "ap" to blocked0.remove("card-9921"), // ap unblocks card-9921 ) counters.forEach { (r, c) -> println("$r sees pending payouts = ${c.value}") } sets.forEach { (r, s) -> println("$r sees blocked cards = ${s.elements}") } println("after the partition heals:") for ((order, c) in orders(counters, PN::merge)) println(" merge $order -> pending payouts = ${c.value}") for ((order, s) in orders(sets, OR::merge)) println(" merge $order -> blocked cards = ${s.elements}") }

try.expect:
eu sees pending payouts = 6
us sees pending payouts = 9
ap sees pending payouts = 4
eu sees blocked cards = [card-9921]
us sees blocked cards = [card-4417, card-5310, card-9921]
ap sees blocked cards = [card-4417]
after the partition heals:
  merge eu + us + ap -> pending payouts = 9
  merge eu + ap + us -> pending payouts = 9
  merge us + eu + ap -> pending payouts = 9
  merge us + ap + eu -> pending payouts = 9
  merge ap + eu + us -> pending payouts = 9
  merge ap + us + eu -> pending payouts = 9
  merge eu + us + ap -> blocked cards = [card-4417, card-5310]
  (the other five orders print the same set)

5 + 3 - 2 + 4 - 1 = 9: every addition and subtraction counted once, in every order. card-9921 is gone, because ap's remove had seen its only tag. card-4417 is back in the set. eu removed tag eu:1, but us had blocked it again with a new tag, us:1, that eu never saw, so the add made at the same time wins. Change one region's edits in the demo, and check that all six orders still agree.

refs.title: crdt.tech: papers, implementations and a glossary of CRDTs

opening:
Picture a shop with two tills and a list of cards to refuse, such as cards reported stolen. Each till keeps its own copy, and the copies sync over the shop's Wi-Fi. One morning the Wi-Fi drops. At the first till, a customer's lost card has turned up, so the cashier takes it off the list. At the second till, the bank phones about a stolen card, and the cashier adds it. When the Wi-Fi comes back, the tills keep the list with the later time on it, the first till's. The stolen card works again, and nobody sees an error.

Keeping the later one feels fair, because on one computer the later write is the newer decision. Here, neither cashier knew about the other's change.

Leaderless replication ended on two writes like these, and copies that kept only one. In this lesson, we'll find a test for when two writes really clash, count what keeping the later one loses, and build two ways to keep both. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two tills whose lists of blocked cards drifted apart while the Wi-Fi was down. Keeping the later list let a stolen card work again, though neither cashier had seen the other's change. Version vectors notice that, and a set that tags every add keeps both changes.

Put a shared shopping-list app on two phones, switch both to airplane mode, and edit the same item on each. Reconnect, and see which rule the app follows: one edit kept, both kept, or a question to you.

That ends the Replication track. Next, in Partitioning, we'll stop copying all the data and start splitting it: what do you do when it no longer fits on one machine?

compare.title: Two concurrent updates: last write wins and vector clocks

a.label: Last write wins (Cassandra)
a.title: Last write wins (Cassandra)
a.html:
capture   status = CAPTURED   ts 10:00:05 (server 2, clock +5 s)
void      status = VOIDED     ts 10:00:02 (server 1, clock right)

every replica keeps the higher timestamp:
  status = CAPTURED
  the void is gone; no error, no sibling, no trace

b.label: Vector clocks (Dynamo)
b.title: Vector clocks (Dynamo)
b.html:
both servers read version [(s1, 1)]
capture   [(s1, 1), (s2, 1)]
void      [(s1, 2)]

compare: s1 is bigger in one, s2 in the other -> CONCURRENT
the next read returns BOTH as siblings:
  CAPTURED [(s1, 1), (s2, 1)]  and  VOIDED [(s1, 2)]
the application decides, and writes back with [(s1, 2), (s2, 1)]

compare.note: Last write wins always produces one answer, so programs never see a conflict, and that's exactly the problem: it decides by clock readings, and one of two concurrent writes disappears. Vector clocks never pick by time. They tell you that two writes didn't see each other, and hand both to your code, which then needs a merge rule that's right for the data. For a payment's status, neither is good enough. A void and a capture shouldn't both be accepted, so the check has to happen before the write (a lightweight transaction or a single leader), not as a merge after it.

worked.title: Choose a conflict rule for four pieces of payment data

steps.say: List the data, and what losing one of two concurrent writes would cost. Be concrete about who notices.
steps.code:
data                 two concurrent writes                  losing one means
merchant display name  two edits in the back office          a stale name, fixed by the next edit
M-0042 payout count    two regions count payouts             a dashboard off by one, forever
blocked cards          eu unblocks, us blocks another card   a fraudster's card works again
payment status         a capture and a void                  money moves that shouldn't

steps.say: The shop's display name, the name customers see, can lose a write: the next edit fixes it. Last write wins is fine here, and it's what Cassandra does anyway, per cell (each single value in a row).
steps.code: merchant display name: LWW per cell (Cassandra's default), no extra code

steps.say: The payout count must keep every change from every region. Make it a PN-Counter: one slot per region for additions and one for subtractions, merged by taking the bigger number in each slot.

The blocked cards must keep both regions' decisions, and a removal must not come back. An OR-Set does that, and an add made at the same time beats a removal, which is the safe side when a card may be stolen.
steps.code:
blocked cards: OR-Set
  add(card) with a fresh tag, remove(card) = the tags seen
  merge = union of tags, union of removed tags

steps.say: The payment's status can't be merged: a capture and a void must not both be accepted. Finding the conflict afterwards is too late, so check before writing, with one leader per payment or a lightweight transaction. In Cassandra, IF makes an UPDATE a lightweight transaction: the replicas first agree, using a voting method called Paxos, that the status is still AUTHORIZED, and the loser of a race is told.
steps.code: UPDATE payments.payment_status SET status = 'VOIDED' WHERE payment_id = 'pay-81723' IF status = 'AUTHORIZED'; -- Paxos: exactly one of capture and void wins, and the loser is told

lab.title: Build vector clocks, a last-write-wins register and three CRDTs
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. All ten fail.
In VectorClock.kt, write compare and merge, then DynamoKey.put. prune, receive and context are written for you. Four tests pass, including Dynamo's D1 to D5 example, replica by replica.

In Crdts.kt, write LwwRegister.merge, for a value that keeps the highest timestamp. Its test passes and shows the skewed-clock loss from the second Try it; the next test shows vector clocks calling the same two writes concurrent.

Write GCounter.merge, then the OR-Set's remove, elements and merge. The last test makes 40 random edits on three replicas, syncs some of them in random directions, and checks that all six merge orders agree, fifty times over.
Experiment: change GCounter.merge to add the slots instead of taking the bigger one, and see which tests fail and why. Put it back.
hints: In compare, loop over counters.keys + other.counters.keys and set two flags: smaller if this[node] < other[node], bigger if >. Both: CONCURRENT. Only smaller: BEFORE. Only bigger: AFTER. Neither: EQUAL.
merge is (counters.keys + other.counters.keys).associateWith { maxOf(this[it], other[it]) }, wrapped in a VectorClock.
put is three lines: Version(value, context.increment(node)), then versions = prune(versions + written), then return it.
LWW: compare timestamp first; on a tie, compare node, so every replica picks the same winner whatever order it merges in.
OR-Set remove adds adds[element].orEmpty() to removed. elements keeps the keys of adds whose tags aren't all in removed. merge unions the tag sets per element, and unions removed.
lab.done: All ten tests in VectorClockTest and CrdtTest pass.

drill.title: Compare vectors and merge counters by hand
drill.prompt: Without running anything, answer: (a) how [(Sx, 2), (Sy, 1)] relates to [(Sx, 2), (Sz, 1)], to [(Sx, 3), (Sy, 1)] and to [(Sx, 3)]; (b) the vector of a write coordinated by Sz whose client read both of the first two; (c) the merge of the G-Counters {eu: 4, us: 2} and {eu: 3, us: 5, ap: 1}, and its value; (d) in one sentence, when two writes are concurrent.

answer.html:
(a) [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,2),(Sz,1)]   CONCURRENT  (bigger on Sy, smaller on Sz)
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,3),(Sy,1)]   BEFORE      (every entry <=, one smaller)
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] vs [(Sx,3)]          CONCURRENT  (smaller on Sx, bigger on Sy)
(b) context = merge = [(Sx,2),(Sy,1),(Sz,1)]; Sz increments its own entry:
    [(Sx,2),(Sy,1),(Sz,2)]
(c) max per slot: {eu: 4, us: 5, ap: 1}, value 10   (adding the slots would give 15: wrong)
(d) When neither writer had seen the other's write when it wrote,
    however far apart their clocks say they were.

recap: Write A happens before write B if B's writer knew about A. Two writes are concurrent when neither happened before the other. It's about knowledge, not time: writes an hour apart can be concurrent, and writes 2 ms apart can be ordered.

Last write wins keeps the highest timestamp, so the copies end up equal, and it silently drops the other concurrent write. Jepsen measured 71.7% of acknowledged writes lost on a healthy Riak cluster when many clients wrote one key (91.4% with a network partition), and none lost with siblings merged as a set. A skewed clock can make even a later write lose.

Version vectors (Dynamo's "vector clocks") keep one counter per replica. Compare them entry by entry: all at most the other's means an ancestor; each bigger somewhere means concurrent, and the store keeps both as siblings for the program to merge.

CRDTs merge with an operation whose order, grouping and repeats don't matter: the G-Counter (the bigger number per slot), the PN-Counter (two G-Counters) and the OR-Set (unique tags; a remove deletes the tags it saw).

The limit: no merge keeps a rule like "a balance never goes below zero". That needs replicas that agree before the write. Which values a read may return at all is where the Consistency and consensus track begins.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "We use last write wins, and our servers' clocks are kept in step, so we always keep the newest decision and never lose anything that matters." Explain what last write wins really keeps, how much it can lose, and what you'd use instead for different kinds of data.
explain.answer: Last write wins keeps whichever version has the highest timestamp, and that's only the newest decision when one writer had seen the other. For concurrent writes, where neither writer knew about the other, there is no newest decision. The clock picks one, and the other write disappears with no error, even though its client was told it succeeded. How much that loses depends on how often writes collide: Jepsen's Riak test, with healthy clocks and no network fault, lost 71.7% of acknowledged writes, because many clients updated one key. Keeping clocks in step doesn't fix that, and when a clock drifts it gets worse, because even a write that had seen the other can lose to it. So it depends on the data. A display name can lose a write, so last write wins is fine. Counts and sets of blocked cards should keep every write, so I'd use CRDTs, a PN-Counter or an OR-Set, or version vectors with siblings and a merge. A payment's status can't be merged at all, because a capture and a void must not both happen, so it needs a check before writing, with a single leader or a lightweight transaction.

deeper.html:
Lamport's 1978 paper defines happens-before, and builds a single counter per program, now called a Lamport clock, that gives every event a number that agrees with it: if A happens before B, A's number is smaller. The reverse fails. A smaller number doesn't mean A happened before B, which is why a Lamport clock can put events in an order but can't spot concurrency. Vector clocks and version vectors fix that by keeping one counter per program. Ordering without a shared clock: logical clocks and IDs, in the Faults, time and truth track, builds both, along with the id schemes that ride on them.

Riak replaced plain version vectors with dotted version vectors, to stop siblings piling up. When many clients write through one node without sending a context, plain vectors can't tell which sibling each write replaces, so the siblings multiply. The "dot" records the single event that created each value. Riak also hands the vector to clients as an opaque "causal context" string that they read and send back, which is the D1 to D5 dance in its production form.

CRDTs come in two styles. State-based CRDTs, the ones in this lesson's lab, send the whole state and merge it. Operation-based CRDTs send each operation instead, and need a delivery layer that delivers every operation exactly once, with each one after the operations it depends on; the text CRDT of Local-first software and sync engines is one. Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero and Zawirski's 2011 report, "A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types", defines both and catalogues counters, registers, sets, graphs and sequences; crdt.tech links it and much more. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6, covers detecting concurrent writes, version vectors and CRDTs alongside the replication styles of this track.
